Features that are too hard to use lead users to work around them, such as writing passwords down
why: Usable security gets used; confusing security gets bypassed.

prompt: Input validation is
options: checking that input is of the expected type, length, format and range before it is used
why: Validation rejects input that does not meet the rules.

prompt: Input sanitisation is
options: checking a password is long enough
cleaning or encoding input so special characters cannot be interpreted as code
why: For example converting < and > to HTML entities before displaying user text.

prompt: Why must validation be done on the server even if the web page already validates with JavaScript?
options: Client-side checks can be bypassed by an attacker sending requests directly
Servers cannot read form data otherwise
It makes the page load faster
why: Client-side validation is for user convenience; server-side validation is for security.

prompt: Which is the most secure way to run this database query in Python?

cur.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + name + "'")

prompt: A login page shows "Password incorrect for user admin" or "No such user". Why is this poor error handling?
options: It tells an attacker which usernames exist
It stops the user logging in
why: A generic message such as "Username or password incorrect" reveals less.

prompt: An application crashes and shows the full stack trace and database file path on the web page. The main security problem is that
options: internal details are exposed that help an attacker
the error message is in English
the user has to reload the page
why: Errors should be logged privately and a generic message shown to the user.

prompt: Static application security testing (SAST)
options: is done by users after release
analyses source code for vulnerabilities without running it
attacks the running application from outside
why: SAST finds issues like unsafe functions early in development.

prompt: Dynamic application security testing (DAST)
options: tests the running application by sending inputs and attacks and observing the responses
reads the source code without running it
is a type of code comment
why: DAST finds problems that only show at runtime, like misconfigured servers.

prompt: Penetration testing is
options: testing that a pen device works
an authorised, simulated attack on a system to find exploitable weaknesses
why: Ethical hackers attempt real attacks with permission and report their findings.

prompt: A code review for security involves
options: other developers reading the code to find vulnerabilities and unsafe practices
why: A second set of eyes catches problems such as missing validation.

prompt: A vulnerability assessment
options: is only done before requirements definition
guarantees the system cannot be hacked
identifies, ranks and reports known weaknesses in a system
why: Unlike penetration testing it does not necessarily exploit them.

prompt: Which describes "fail securely" error handling?
options: Errors are ignored so the program keeps running
If an error occurs, the user is logged in as admin
All errors are displayed in full to the user
If something goes wrong, the system denies access rather than allowing it
why: A failed permission check must not leave the door open.

prompt: Business continuity and disaster recovery plans are needed because
options: they set out how to keep operating and restore data and systems after a breach or failure
they replace the need for backups
why: Resilience means planning for the attack that succeeds.

prompt: An attacker types ' OR '1'='1 into a login form and gets in without a password. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: User input was inserted into a SQL statement and changed its meaning.

prompt: A forum post contains a hidden script that runs in every visitor's browser and sends their session cookie to the attacker. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: Untrusted text was sent to other users' browsers without encoding, so it ran as script.

prompt: A logged-in bank customer visits a malicious page that silently submits a transfer form to their bank using their session. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: The victim's browser sent their valid session with a request they never intended to make.

prompt: A website's link /go?url=... sends users to any address in the query string, which phishers use to send people to fake sites. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: The site redirects to an address taken from the request without checking it is allowed.

prompt: Two purchase requests arrive at the same moment and both see one ticket in stock, so the ticket is sold twice. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: The result depended on the timing of two operations on shared data.

prompt: A website never expires session IDs and puts them in the URL, so an attacker reuses a copied link to act as the user. Which vulnerability or attack is this?

prompt: An attacker measures how long a password check takes to work out how many characters were correct. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: Information leaked through a physical or timing side effect, not through a flaw in the logic itself.

prompt: An upload form accepts a file named ../../config.py and overwrites a server file. Which vulnerability or attack is this?

prompt: A search page displays the search term from the URL without encoding it, so a crafted link runs script for whoever clicks it. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: Untrusted text was sent to other users' browsers without encoding, so it ran as script.

prompt: An attacker uploads a file called photo.jpg that is really an executable script, which the server then runs. Which vulnerability or attack is this?
why: The server trusted the file name instead of checking the file's real type and never executing uploads.

prompt: Which is the best defence against cross-site scripting (XSS)?
options: Encoding output so user text is displayed as text, plus a Content Security Policy
why: This removes the cause of the attack rather than its symptoms.

prompt: Which is the best defence against race conditions?
options: Locking or atomic transactions so only one process can update shared data at a time
why: This removes the cause of the attack rather than its symptoms.

prompt: Which is the best defence against broken session management?

prompt: Which is the best defence against invalid redirects?

Only redirecting to addresses on an approved allow list
why: This removes the cause of the attack rather than its symptoms.

prompt: Which is the best defence against timing side-channel attacks on password checks?

Comparing secrets in constant time so the check takes the same time whether it fails early or late
why: This removes the cause of the attack rather than its symptoms.

the server stores passwords in plain text
the victim types the attacker's password
the page contains a SQL query

prompt: Stored XSS differs from reflected XSS because stored XSS

is a type of SQL injection
needs physical access to the server

prompt: Brute-force login attacks are best reduced by

prompt: Which is a benefit of collaboration when developing secure software?

giving every task to the team leader

prompt: Which is an enterprise benefit of developing secure software?

how organisations collect, use, store and disclose personal information

prompt: The Notifiable Data Breaches scheme requires an organisation covered by the Privacy Act to
options: notify affected people and the regulator when a breach is likely to cause serious harm

options: the legal rights over creations such as source code, designs and algorithms
the hardware the software runs on

prompt: How can secure software development affect employment?

It means only managers are needed
It has no effect on jobs

Version control with commits linked to each developer and reviewed before merging
Allowing anyone to push directly to production

take reasonable steps to ensure the overseas recipient handles the data consistently with the Australian Privacy Principles

prompt: Which is a social issue caused by a major data breach?
